heading: Security
body:
Every response carries defensive security headers. One of them is a strict content security policy. This header tells the browser which content the page may load. The policy is `script-src 'self'`, no inline script, `object-src 'none'` and `frame-ancestors 'none'`. The only inline script is the speculation rules block, which lets the browser fetch a linked page before the click. The policy allows it by the SHA-256 hash of its text, which every browser understands. Chrome's own keyword for it, `'inline-speculation-rules'`, made Safari warn on every page and refuse the block. The Windows and Linux desktop hosts build their policy from the same source, so their web views allow the same scripts, the hash included; their policy also allows images, fonts and connections over `https:`. A controller call runs as one process with limits: a deadline and a concurrency limit (the most requests it runs at the same time). Its protocol frames (the messages it exchanges with the server) are limited to 16 MiB. The server checks each argument against the types of the controller method. This happens before Tachyon calls the method.

Every route says who may call it (`Public`, `SignedIn` or `Allow(Role)`), and one `IdentityProvider` class says who is signed in. The server answers 401 or 403 before the method runs (see Who may call a route). How users sign in stays with the application: the identity provider reads a session or a token in the language's own request type. Tachyon has no CORS (cross-origin resource sharing) layer; a middleware runs its `before` method before every request, and that policy goes there. The policy's `connect-src` allows the page's own origin and the hosts in `tac.outgoing.hosts` only.
